#46235. Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that finding love is substantial business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business.
  • The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages.
  • According to recent reports, as a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this newly introduced generation of dating apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that finding love is substantial business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app customers to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

According to recent reports, as a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this newly introduced generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

Industry observers note that so if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

What about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user states they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

It has been revealed that what do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

Industry observers note that the truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Industry observers note that with the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

According to recent reports, I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

Industry observers note that an alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

In a recent development, amie M. Gordon, Ph.D., is a social-personality psychologist who takes a dynamic, dyadic approach to investigating the affective, social-cognitive, and biological processes that shape interpersonal relationships. Her research has been published in top academic journals as well as featured in popular news outlets such as The Newly introduced York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Atlantic. She received her PhD in Social-Personality Psychology from UC Berkeley and her BA in Psychology from UCLA. She blogs for Psychology Today in Between You and Me, and is at the moment completing a postdoctoral research fellowship at the University of California, San Francisco.

Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Upcoming Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852.
  • The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back.
  • “What happened this July was really special,” says George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Upcoming Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.

The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.

“What happened this July was really special,” says George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.

According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.

According to recent reports, “It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke indicates. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”.

According to recent reports, according to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker indicates. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”.

Things moved promptly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director states.

According to recent reports, after the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.

“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree claims, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.

In a recent development, baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker states, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.

“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker says, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”.

#46233. Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2322 w)

Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles.
  • That’s just your teens becoming independent.
  • It has been revealed that none of this is easy, of course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles. In the teen years, sweet hugs can provoke eye rolls; a well-intentioned “How was your day?” may be misconstrued as meddling.

That’s just your teens becoming independent. Decades of research finds that portraying adolescence as a period of “storm and stress” is not only misguided, it’s harmful. In fact, developmental science shows this time of life is better recast as “the breakthrough years.” According to research on over one thousand adolescents by Ellen Galinsky, author and president of Families and Work Institute, there are key messages that teens want to get through to adults:.

It has been revealed that none of this is easy, of course. Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do. Here are common questions, with answers backed by scientists and their research.

In a recent development, Q: My 16-year-old doesn’t seem to be motivated to do anything beyond hanging out with friends and playing video games. When I bring up the prospect of college, he notes he doesn’t care. What should I do?

A: As parents, we want to set our high schoolers up for success. But, at that age, young people are still trying to figure out who they are, what interests them, and what their future looks like. “Identity development and purpose formation are underway, but rarely fully formed by high school,” says Kendall Cotton Bronk, professor of psychology at Claremont Graduate University.

Not finding any answers yet is expected. “Parents need to remind themselves that where their child is at this moment in time isn’t necessarily where they will be in the future,” says Bronk.

According to recent reports, to help teens along, encourage them to try different activities at school and in the community, whether it’s, for instance, robotics, the debate team, chorus, improv, or the school paper. Leave it to them to select what to try. Don’t do it for them. Don’t judge their choices.

Sources indicate that “While it’s not appropriate for parents to be too directive, they can help their teenager reflect on what they liked and didn’t like and what felt meaningful and not so meaningful about their various experiences,” says Bronk. “Having someone to debrief with can help them deepen their reflection and more quickly identify a purposeful direction.”.

Research suggests that when teens are guided by their own interests, free of external pressures, they’re more likely to take charge of their own career development. But when parents are overly involved in their adolescents’ lives, indicates Bronk, young people don’t have an opportunity to cultivate a sense of agency, and this can make career development planning a major challenge.

Instead of trying to manage their path, indicates Bronk, parents should simply “be curious.” Ask your child: What interests you? What feels satisfying for you?

Recent findings suggest that “This kind of questioning can scaffold and deepen their young person’s reflections, and reflection is a key component of figuring out what kind of path a young person wants to follow,” she notes. “Usually, what holds their interest is something they’re good at and care about, and that allows them to make a meaningful difference in the broader world,” she explains.

Taking advantage of volunteer opportunities can help young people see themselves as useful and discover careers that might interest them—for instance, helping out in a food pantry, animal shelter, a kids sports organization, or hospital. Encourage your teen to ask people he knows about their jobs, what they entail, and what they studied to get there.

Finally, don’t assume that your child’s lack of direction is apathy. Whatever their interest is, “work with it, not against it,” notes Bronk. “At the same time, be patient. It may just be the case that they haven’t figured it all out yet. Their timetable may not be the same as yours, but they will eventually get there. Remember, this isn’t a race.”.

It has been revealed that Q: My 15-year-old seems to be living a separate life. He spends most of his time in his room and has dinner more often with his friends than with us. How can we encourage him to be a part of the family?

A: Seeking independence (while still navigating being dependent on adults) is one of the primary tasks of adolescents as they transition to becoming more self-sufficient into early adulthood.

“I try to get parents to understand that it’s not about them,” indicates Laurence Steinberg, author of You and Your Adolescent. “The parents didn’t do anything wrong; the child isn’t rejecting them. This is a sign they’re growing up normally. It’s partly wanting to make their own decisions and have their own life, but it’s also wanting emotional independence—to show that they are more than their parents’ kid.”.

Chances are a closed door doesn’t mean trouble. Just as most adults don’t want others listening in on their calls, teens don’t want that either. They’re not distancing themselves from you, but simply distancing themselves from being a child.

“There’s nothing the parents can do to stop this from happening,” says Steinberg, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. “And they shouldn’t try.”.

In a recent development, that mentioned, spending time with family is also vital. To suggest that, say something like, “We want to spend more time with you, but we also know that spending time with friends is important. What’s the best way to catch up with you?” By making the planning of it a collaborative process, your child is more likely to stay engaged. Research suggests that they may even find the activity more enjoyable.

In a recent development, only rarely is a shut bedroom door cause for concern—for instance, you notice other behavioral changes, such as a drop in grades, a dwindling interest in his usual in-person activities. If you suspect an problem, let your child know that you’re there for him, and that he can get professional help, too.

Sources indicate that one last note: If your child is spending most of his time in his room online, setting limits on its own may not be enough, notes Jacqueline Nesi, author of the Techno Sapiens newsletter and associate professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University. You’ll also want to discuss with them what you want for him and what he wants.

The evidence also supports “co-viewing” or “co-using” technology with your kids, whether that’s a video game, TV, or an AI chatbot, says Nesi. Using tech together can spark conversation and help parents better understand their kids’ digital lives.

In a recent development, that said, it’s still notable for you to protect their sleep and to make sure that they live a life in person. Again, to get their buy-in, decide on screen-time parameters, and replace screen time with in-person activities he might enjoy, such cooking a favorite meal together or an outing with family and friends.

Q: My 17-year-old daughter recently suffered a breakup. How can I help her feel better without intruding?

According to recent reports, A: Even if a relationship doesn’t look like a monogamous romantic relationship in adulthood (it may be short, or the partners may not talk to each other very much), these breakups can still be painful. So always take your teen’s romantic activities seriously, as well as the emotions they are experiencing following a breakup, says Emily Bibby, a researcher at the Relationship Development Center at Stony Brook University. Be compassionate, validating, and nonjudgmental. Let her know that she is having a normal reaction to a difficult situation.

Allow space to grieve and vent. “Listen hard to what your child is thinking and feeling,” claims Barry Farber, professor of psychology and education at Columbia University Teachers College. “Ask what they’ve learned from the relationship. Framing the relationship as a learning experience, as opposed to a failure, can help nurture resilience and personal growth, and can help her feel more in control and more hopeful about future relationships.”.

Industry observers note that as Farber and his coauthors point out in a recent study, while time doesn’t necessarily “heal all wounds” (because memories and thoughts can linger), it almost always “softens the blow” when other strategies are also employed, such as talking with a trusted friend or family member. While the study involved mostly white, female adult subjects, the same principle generally applies across ages, genders, and ethnicities. Letting your child know that things will get better can help.

Trying to convince a teen to do anything is difficult, notes Farber, so it’s better to simply listen, and then only encourage as opposed to insisting or dictating. Encourage her to engage in activities she enjoys, whether it’s treating herself to an afternoon manicure, going to a concert, or spending time in nature like hiking and walking on the beach. Encourage her to avoid all contact with her ex, both in person and on social media. If one person believes it’s really over, a clean break is usually best, says Farber. Any surge of adrenaline that happens when you see your ex in any form is only temporary, and only makes it harder to get over the breakup.

According to recent reports, if sad feelings are impairing day-to-day life—she’s not seeing friends, she’s failing her classes, there’s a dramatic change in eating or sleeping—have her consider seeking help from a mental health professional. “Therapy normalizes the experience,” indicates Farber. “It helps people find a upcoming narrative when they’re stuck.”.

Therapy also gives people an opportunity to share their feelings in a private space and learn evidence-based emotion-regulation skills to improve their mental health and functioning, claims Bibby.

This workbook is for a range of practitioners who support parents and caregivers of children between preschool and high school.

If your teen is debilitatingly depressed or harming herself, then advise that she get professional help as soon as possible, such as from her school psychologist, her primary care doctor (for a referral), or a therapist you think highly of.

According to recent reports, to help their teen navigate relationships in general, parents can model healthy relationships with not just a partner, but also friends and family members. Teaching your teen effective communication skills and boundary setting early on, in the context of friendships and family relationships, can prove helpful once your teen starts dating, says Bibby, who recently coauthored a research review on romantic relationships and mental health in adolescents.

Recent findings suggest that and as for parents of teens who are just becoming interested in dating, it’s helpful to talk about what healthy relationships look like, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect. “Thinking through what they would do [in different dating scenarios] and how to navigate different challenges that may arise can build confidence when they start dating,” claims Bibby.

Q: My 14-year-old has found herself in a friend group that spends a lot of money on expensive clothing and electronics. We don’t approve of these teens and don’t share their consumerist values. How do we prevent our child from becoming materialistic, too?

Industry observers note that A: You can empower your teen to make thoughtful, confident choices about money, friendships, and the pressures they face. Try leading with connection rather than control: Talk openly about your family’s values, help them practice setting boundaries, and remind them they do not need to match their friends’ spending to belong or feel worthy. Expensive tastes and social media pressures can be hard to ignore, but your teen can learn to make choices that reflect what matters most to them.

People turn to materialistic things to fill a void, but that’s only a temporary fix, says Lan Nguyen Chaplin, a professor of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University, and an expert in children’s and teens’ consumer behavior. “They end up in a vicious cycle of wanting and needing more to fill the same void because material things cannot fill real voids.”.

Industry observers note that in her research exploring materialism in a group of 12- to 18-year-olds, she reported that those with high self-esteem were less likely to have materialistic tendencies. “Parents and peers [are] a source of emotional support and psychological well-being,” she writes. “Supportive parents and peers boost adolescents’ self-esteem, which decreases their need to turn to material goods to develop positive self-perceptions.”.

Industry observers note that read this article in Spanish on La Red Hispana, the public-facing media outlet and distribution house of HCN, focused on educating, inspiring, and informing 40 million U.S. Hispanics.

To that end, start at home and help your kids feel good about themselves. Gratitude journals can be a good way to curb materialism, but, of course, asking a teen who is new to journaling to start one can feel like a homework writing assignment if it’s yet another thing they are required to do. Rather, approach it with a light touch. Model gratitude by sharing with your teen who and what you’re grateful for, keep a gratitude journal yourself, or ask them what the high point of their day is.

It also helps to stop tying accomplishments to material things. So, instead of, say, rewarding a good report card with money or sneakers, celebrate the hard work that was put into achieving the good grades over a fun experience together like a movie night at home.

Most of all, spend time with your teen in lighthearted and playful ways, no matter how short. Even a 10-minute car ride can be a good opportunity to connect with them, and also reinforce the good things they have going for them, Chaplin says.

Joanne Chen is a writer and editor in Fresh York City. Her articles on children and parenting have appeared in The Bump, Parents Magazine, and the New York Times.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report.
  • Screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite reveals.
  • Industry observers note that conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report. You wince at the number, then swipe it away with the same thumb you were scrolling with.

Screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite reveals. By evening, you can feel worn out even if the day wasn’t particularly busy.

Industry observers note that conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them. A few small tweaks to your daily routine are a good place to start. Below, you’ll find some realistic ways to cut back, plus a look at why it can feel so hard to put your phone down.

Recent findings suggest that there's no set amount of time that counts as too much. What matters more is how your screen use affects you. Signs worth noticing include strained eyes, restless sleep, reaching for your phone out of habit, and feeling worse after scrolling. If any of these sound familiar, the tips below may help.

Sources indicate that 💙 Not sure if this sounds like you? Check out these five signs you might be online too much.

If “one more video” keeps turning into one more hour, you’re in good tech giant. Many apps are designed to keep you scrolling, so you’ll need more than willpower to cut back. Start with one or two tips that feel doable right now. You can come back to the rest later.

It has been revealed that bright colors can make apps harder to put down, and notification badges and thumbnails are built to draw you in. Switching your screen to black and white takes away some of that appeal, which can make scrolling feel less rewarding.

Try: Search “grayscale” or “color filters” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under Accessibility or Well-Being.

Grayscale may look odd for a day or two. Some people keep it on all day, and others only turn it on in the evening to wind down. You can turn it off whenever you need to, like when you’re using maps or looking at photos.

According to recent reports, 💙 Listen to the Build Healthier Phone Habits series with Dr. Aditi Nerurkar on Calm.

In a recent development, time can slip by while you scroll. Set a daily limit on your one or two most-used apps, and your phone will nudge you when you reach it.

Try: Search “app limits” or “app timers” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under screen time.

Industry observers note that start with a limit slightly below how much you use those apps now, then lower it gradually. Smaller steps are often more sustainable than cutting back all at once.

Notifications like news alerts, app promos, social likes, and game reminders mostly add noise. Keep the ones you rely on, such as texts, calls, and reminders, and turn off the rest.

Try: Search “notifications” in your device settings, then toggle off the alerts you don’t need, starting with the apps that send the most.

Constant check-ins can keep you glued to your screens all day. Pick a few set times to go through your messages, emails, and feeds.

Try: Limit your check-ins to lunchtime and after work, and keep your personal devices out of reach in between.

Before you open your phone, take one slow breath and ask yourself why you’re reaching for it. If the answer is just habit, that brief pause may be enough to snap you out of autopilot.

Try: Breathe in for four counts and out for six, then see if you still want to unlock your phone.

💙 Discover 10 types of breathing exercises you can try anytime, anywhere.

When you feel the urge to pick up your phone, try turning to an offline activity instead. Keep an activity you enjoy within reach, like a book on the couch or a sketchpad on the table.

According to recent reports, 💙 Want to work on the habit before the urge hits? Explore Tame Your Scrolling Habit with Rose Nisker on Calm.

It has been revealed that choose one or two spots to keep screen-free, such as the dinner table or your bedroom. A clear boundary often works better than a vague promise to use screens less. These zones also give you room to be more present, like during a family meal or your evening wind-down.

Try: Place your phone in a dedicated spot, like a basket by the door. If you share a home, invite everyone to join.

💙 Not ready to go phone-free at night? Tune in to Sleeping with Your Phone with Dr. Matthew Walker on Calm.

Pick a cutoff time for all your screens, such as 30 minutes before bed, and stick to it as best you can. Late-night screen use can keep your mind active and make it harder to fall asleep.

If you usually watch a TV show before bed, choose one episode and turn off autoplay.

Try: Schedule a nightly reminder for your cutoff. Swap your screen time for a calming activity, like journaling or a short meditation.

💙 Press play on the Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

A few common app features can keep you hooked:.

Infinite scroll: New posts keep loading, so you never reach a natural stopping point.

Autoplay: The next video or episode starts on its own, which keeps you watching unless you stop it.

Unpredictable notifications: Each message or like feels like a small reward, and not knowing when the next one will pop up keeps you checking.

Sources indicate that your emotions play a part too. A screen can be a quick escape when you’re stressed or putting something off. It can bring relief in the moment, even if you feel more drained afterward.

💙 If your screen time has been weighing on your mood, read our guide on what to do if technology is impacting your mental health.

Sources indicate that if you want to cut back on screen time without giving up after a few days, start small. Choose one change, like keeping your phone off the dinner table, and give yourself time to adjust before you make another tweak to your routine. If you slip back into old habits, you can always start again the next day.

To set screen time limits that stick, build them into your routine so you don’t have to rely on willpower in the moment. You could use an app timer or set aside a screen-free time each day, like the first half hour after you wake up.

There isn’t a daily screen time limit that works for every adult. If you’d like to use screens less, a good starting point is a limit slightly below your current daily average, and you can lower that limit gradually as you get used to it.

How you spend your screen time matters just as much. An hour on a video call with a friend often leaves you feeling better than an hour of doomscrolling.

You can reduce your screen time at night by setting a cutoff time before bed and charging your phone across the room. Swap your late-night scroll for a book or a short meditation to help you relax before sleep.

In a recent development, to help your family reduce screen time together, make it a shared strategy. You could agree on screen-free times, such as during meals or the first hour after school or work. Try leading by example, rather than telling your kids or partner what to do.

Recent findings suggest that no, you don’t have to quit screens completely to feel better. Technology connects you to the people and things you care about. You can cut back on the screen use that leaves you feeling worse, like aimless scrolling, and keep what you value.

In a recent development, mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

Industry observers note that “Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.
  • Industry observers note that researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels.
  • The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new type of brain implant could give scientists a more precise way to study the brain and may eventually contribute to treatments for neurological conditions such as epilepsy.

Industry observers note that researchers from DTU, the University of Copenhagen, University College London, and other institutions have developed a long, needle-thin brain electrode equipped with microscopic channels. Known as the microfluidic Axialtrode (mAxialtrode), the device is designed to provide multiple functional points along the length of the implant. This allows researchers to record neural activity and deliver medication to specific locations across different parts of the brain.

The findings were published in the journal Advanced Science.

A Multifunction Tool for Brain Research.

For now, the technology is primarily intended as a research tool. Scientists could use it to investigate how signals travel through different layers of the brain during processes involving epilepsy, memory, and decision-making.

Over the longer term, the researchers say the mAxialtrode could also have therapeutic applications. One possibility would be using the device to deliver drugs to precise locations while simultaneously applying electrical stimulation or light stimulation to selected areas of the brain.

Postdoc Kunyang Sui, who developed the mAxialtrode concept together with Associate Professor Christos Markos, says one of the main advantages is that several capabilities can be combined within a single implant. That could allow researchers to perform more precise experiments while reducing the need for multiple devices inserted into the brain.

Sources indicate that "Most current brain implants are based on hard materials such as silicon, which can irritate the brain and trigger inflammatory reactions in the tissue. The fresh implant differs in that it is made of soft, plastic-like optical fibers and has a specially angled tip that makes it smaller and reduces the damage caused when it is placed in the brain," notes Kunyang Sui.

In a recent development, sui cautions that the technology is still far from routine clinical use. Extensive testing, additional development, and regulatory approvals would be required before it could be used to treat patients.

Moving Beyond Conventional Optical Fibers.

Recent findings suggest that brain researchers presently use flat-ended optical fibers in many experiments. These thin fibers, made from glass or plastic, can carry light into deep regions of the brain. They are frequently used in optogenetics, a technique in which specific nerve cells are activated using light.

Conventional fibers, however, have an vital limitation. They typically interact with brain tissue only at the end of the fiber, meaning researchers can stimulate or monitor just one location at a time.

In a recent development, the outermost end is called the distal tip, or the "nose" of the fiber. Light is emitted and contact with brain tissue occurs only at this point. As a result, scientists may be limited to measuring or stimulating one brain layer at a time, even though many brain functions depend on communication among several layers and deeper structures.

How the New Brain Implant Works.

The needle-thin mAxialtrode begins as a much larger polymer rod. Researchers heat the material and draw it into an extremely thin fiber, somewhat like producing a very fine strand of sugar, but with far greater precision.

According to recent reports, A light-conducting core runs through the center of the fiber. Surrounding it are eight microscopic channels that can transport liquids. Those channels can also hold extremely thin metal wires used to measure electrical activity in the brain.

According to recent reports, the finished fiber measures less than half a millimeter across. It is also highly flexible, allowing it to move along with brain tissue rather than pressing rigidly through it. This difference in stiffness could be crucial because harder implants can trigger inflammatory responses when they remain in the brain for long periods.

The researchers tested the system not only in the laboratory but also "in vivo," meaning in living mice. The electrode was implanted in the animals' brains and connected to light sources, recording equipment, and small pumps used to deliver fluids.

The experiments demonstrated that the device could stimulate nerve cells using both blue and red light. At the same time, researchers were able to record electrical activity from shallow and deeper brain regions, including the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.

Industry observers note that they were also able to inject different substances at separate depths, with delivery points spaced almost three millimeters apart. All of these measurements and forms of stimulation were carried out using a single lightweight fiber, which the mice were able to carry without any obvious signs of discomfort.

Potential Applications in Epilepsy and Neuroscience.

In a recent development, the in vivo experiments and neurophysiological validation were performed in close collaboration with Associate Professor Rune W. Berg of the University of Copenhagen and Associate Professor Rob C. Wykes from University College London. Their contributions included expertise in analyzing neural circuits and models relevant to epilepsy.

The research team is now working to patent the technology behind the brain electrode. The scientists are also exploring what would be required to begin testing the device in patients within a clinical setting.

#46229. Industry News: As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?

Industry News: As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions.
  • Recent findings suggest that another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging.
  • In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the New Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’” Carstensen was clear that the center’s aim was not to increase lifespans—which had nearly doubled during the 20th century—but rather to build societies that accommodated that new and unprecedented reality.

Recent findings suggest that another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging. As Carstensen noted often, “Longevity is not synonymous with aging. It is a metric of length.” The center’s interest is in the challenges and opportunities that longer lives present. While the center is keenly interested in older people, in Carstensen’s view, “longer lives have implications for every stage of life, and the roots of many problems faced at advanced ages have their roots much earlier in life.” The center’s mission is to use longer lives to improve quality of life at all ages.

In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the New Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies. After nearly 20 years, Carstensen, the Fairleigh S. Dickinson Jr. Professor in Public Policy and a professor of psychology at Stanford, will step down this summer from her role at the Stanford Center on Longevity to pursue a new project alongside her research and teaching.

According to recent reports, I spoke with Carstensen about what she’s learned along the way and what’s next. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Karen Breslau: What’s changed since the center’s early days?

Laura Carstensen: I hope it’s clearer that the aging process has not changed much, if any, genetically over the last several thousand years. Rather, longevity—the length of life—increased, and that has enormous implications for nearly all aspects of our lives. The modifiability of aging, on the other hand, is also clear. Even though we’re essentially the same physiological beings that our ancestors were, we changed the world in ways that are allowing us to live healthier and longer. That’s why we are confident that we can build a world where the majority of people live well for a century.

In a recent development, KB: You are on the scientific advisory council to the Health District of Singapore, which is building the Queenstown Health District, a very intentional all-ages community that is incorporating principles from the Upcoming Map of Life. What are you seeing?

LC: The Singapore government has given a group of scientists the freedom to design a neighborhood in ways that support long-term health and intergenerational connections, continued financial security, and exercise. They’re thinking about all the factors that contribute to long, healthy, and engaged lives and literally programming them into the community. What’s really cool about the Queenstown Health District is that it can provide a proof of concept that social and physical designs can improve long life.

Already they have built parks and playgrounds with swings for the kids and balance beams for older residents, to provide shared spaces where different ages interact. When we advisers fly in from different countries, we’re starry-eyed at what they can do. Singapore can do things like this in part because they’re smaller, and their government can act quickly. For example, the government recognized about a decade ago that people weren’t saving enough for retirement. So they flipped a switch and said, “OK, everybody’s putting in more money into their retirement account.”.

According to recent reports, KB: If you had to give a grade to where the U.S. is in implementing the Upcoming Map of Life principles, could you take out your red pen?

LC: Compared to some countries, like Singapore, I’d give the U.S. a C-minus, and I am used to grade inflation! The federal government has done little to improve longevity. Unlike the Singapore government, which can require people to save more for retirement, for example, the U.S. cannot quickly implement such programs. On the other hand, in part because the government contributes less, we see a lot of innovation coming from the private sector. We have entire industries offering fresh products and services. So I’m optimistic about what the U.S. can contribute to longevity. At a global level, it’s fabulous to think about the different approaches that can come from the public and private sectors in a range of countries.

KB: Longevity has gone mainstream and led to billions of dollars in market interest. How has that changed the center’s work?

Industry observers note that LC: It’s true that vast investments are going to longevity. Most of these funds are directed at ways that individuals can live longer. There isn’t, in my experience, much philanthropic interest in this space aimed at helping people live better as we live longer lives. I am discouraged that we are sleepwalking through this seismic demographic shift without investing more in the opportunity to rewrite the life scripts that have guided life and imagining ways that we could use them to improve life.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also discouraging that as longevity has entered public consciousness, much of what we hear about are pitches for questionable products that supposedly make people live longer. There are so many snake-oil salesmen in this space that it’s hard for consumers to distinguish what is evidence-based and what is not.

KB: As you often say, transitions are a feature of longer lives. What’s happening next for you?

According to recent reports, LC: I’m going to focus more on research and teaching, but first I’m going on sabbatical and look forward to having more time for the things I love—my garden, being at home, sitting in the sun, going for walks. I want to take Pilates lessons. I’m going to take a break in my schedule to say, “How do I create a healthy lifestyle going forward and build the rest around it?”.

Industry observers note that while I hopefully will have a more relaxed schedule, during my sabbatical I’ll be developing an online course called The Fundamentals of Longevity, which will tell the story of longevity and the potential to live longer, better lives, a change we really need in the world. The course will be accessible far beyond Stanford, so that we can help frame the conversation around longevity and help people appreciate the extraordinary promise of science, technology, and social change to improve life. There is a crisis on the horizon if we don’t change the way we live.

Recent findings suggest that we have the opportunity to change our lives for the better. We have opportunities no previous generation of humans in history has had, and we need to start implementing them.

#46228. Breaking: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📅 22 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (780 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep.
  • According to recent reports, to investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity.
  • "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep. Some people can have caffeine late in the day and fall asleep easily, while others may remain awake for hours. But researchers are increasingly finding that simply asking whether coffee delays sleep may miss a more key problem: what caffeine does to the brain after sleep begins.

According to recent reports, to investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity. EEG measurements can reveal much more than how long someone sleeps or how often they wake up. They can also provide clues about the biological quality and depth of that sleep.

"EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping. Classical sleep assessment assesses sleep duration and its stages, whereas quantitative EEG analysis reveals more subtle changes, such as reduced slow-wave activity, which is an important marker of sleep depth and its restorative character," explains Prof. Donata Kurpas from the Department of Nursing, Wroclaw Medical University.

Slow waves are a major feature of deep sleep -- the stage associated with physical recovery, replenishing energy reserves, and maintaining healthy brain function.

Caffeine May Make Sleep Less Restorative.

According to recent reports, caffeine does not always affect sleep in obvious ways. A person may still fall asleep at a normal time and remain asleep for what appears to be a full night, yet the quality of that rest may still be altered.

"Caffeine may shorten sleep or make it more difficult to fall asleep; however, even when sleep duration appears normal, it may reduce slow-wave activity and shift the EEG pattern toward a more 'wakeful' brain," indicates Prof. Kurpas.

Sources indicate that in practical terms, someone might spend eight hours in bed without getting the same level of neurological recovery they would normally expect. Because the disruption may not cause obvious awakenings, it can easily go unnoticed.

Industry observers note that "The subjective feeling of having slept well does not always correspond to what we observe in neurophysiological recordings. A person may fall asleep without major difficulty and not remember awakenings, while the brain may display fewer features of deep sleep," the expert adds.

Why Caffeine Affects People Differently.

Industry observers note that another major finding from caffeine research is that responses vary considerably from person to person. Genetics, metabolism, age, stress, and chronic fatigue can all influence how strongly caffeine affects sleep.

For some people, even coffee consumed early in the day may still have an impact by nighttime.

"It is not only about coffee consumed just before bedtime. For some people, the total amount of caffeine consumed during the day and whether the body has enough time to metabolize it before nightfall may also be important," Prof. Kurpas emphasizes.

That possibility may be especially relevant for people who rely on caffeine to improve focus, stamina, or performance, including athletes, people doing mentally demanding work, and anyone who regularly uses coffee or other caffeinated products to stay alert.

Caffeine Can Create a Fatigue Cycle.

Recent findings suggest that caffeine can temporarily increase alertness and make fatigue feel less noticeable. However, experts caution that the boost may sometimes come at the expense of the body's ability to recover fully during sleep.

Industry observers note that in that sense, caffeine can resemble "borrowing energy" from the body. If nighttime recovery becomes less effective, the person may feel more tired the following day and turn to even more caffeine for help.

It has been revealed that "If caffeine helps a person function during the day while simultaneously worsening the quality of nighttime recovery, a vicious circle may develop: greater fatigue, greater need for stimulation, and poorer sleep," says Prof. Kurpas.

Industry observers note that these findings are one reason sleep researchers are paying less attention to sleep duration alone. Increasingly, the focus is shifting toward what the brain is actually doing during the night and whether that sleep is biologically restorative.

According to recent reports, "Caffeine is neither 'good' nor 'bad'. It is a biologically active substance whose effects depend on dose, time of day, age, lifestyle, sleep quality, stress burden, and individual sensitivity," the expert concludes.

Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me.
  • Recent findings suggest that often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors.
  • For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Recent findings suggest that often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

According to recent reports, at Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

It has been revealed that at Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

Back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Sources indicate that of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

In a recent development, it’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins states these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”.

Mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

Mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something fresh. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

Industry observers note that it was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty.

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible.

As I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.

Sources indicate that in our Dickinson College episode, that choice shows up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates. Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.

The choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.

According to recent reports, here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part.

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.

Sources indicate that but the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur.

I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

At Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences.

Sources indicate that the series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones.

It has been revealed that in my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

Sources indicate that I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an issue than a conversation built only around agreement.

In a recent development, lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

Industry observers note that when Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates new points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

According to recent reports, at the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang.

It has been revealed that working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

Industry observers note that for example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III.

Sources indicate that if you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social issues, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It indicates that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

Sources indicate that iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco.

Recent findings suggest that I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

As another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too important to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

#46225. When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (674 w)
